# Barycentric density selection above a prescribed law in convex order

This note proves an all-dimensional replacement for the one-dimensional
comonotone selection used in
`candidate a60ee1969152d817` and
`candidate 229cbb48c7fa3080`.
The selected law depends on the prescribed old law. No greatest law in
multidimensional convex order is asserted. This is a transport selection
theorem, not a proof of OC or a parity packing theorem.

## 1. Statement and conventions

Let m>=1 and k>=1. Let gamma_1,...,gamma_k be compactly supported finite
positive Borel measures on R^m, all with mass M, and suppose

    gamma_i <= a_i Leb_m,       0<a_i<infinity.

Let lambda_i>0 have sum one. A coupling pi of these measures is a finite
positive measure on (R^m)^k having ith marginal gamma_i. Write

    b(x_1,...,x_k)=sum_i lambda_i x_i,
    rho_pi=b_*pi,
    A=(sum_i lambda_i a_i^(-1/m))^(-m).             (1)

**Theorem.** For every such coupling pi_0 there is a coupling pi of the
same marginals such that

    rho_pi <= A Leb_m,
    rho_pi0 <=_cx rho_pi.                           (2)

Here alpha<=_cx beta means that the measures have the same finite mass
and that integral f d alpha <= integral f d beta for every finite convex
function f:R^m->R. These functions are continuous, and all integrals in
this note are finite because the relevant supports are compact. Equal
first moments also follow directly from the fixed marginals.

In particular, if k=2, lambda_1=lambda_2=1/2, and a_1=a_2=1, the new
midpoint law is dominated by Leb_m and dominates the old midpoint law
in convex order. Neither the old coupling nor its conditional kernels
need remain fixed. The same conclusion holds for every k with a_i=1.

If M=0 all measures are zero and the assertion is immediate. We assume
M>0 below. Zero barycentric weights, if allowed, can simply be discarded.

The constant A is sharp; Section 7 gives an exact example.

## 2. Compact continuous-cost duality with attainment

We record the version needed here, including a proof to make all
attainment issues explicit. Let K_i be nonempty compact subsets of
Euclidean spaces, let gamma_i have common mass M>0 and support in K_i,
and let c be a Lipschitz function on their product. There exist an
optimal coupling pi and continuous functions u_i on K_i satisfying

    sum_i u_i(x_i) >= c(x_1,...,x_k),               (3)
    sum_i integral u_i d gamma_i = integral c d pi
                               = max_pi' integral c d pi'. (4)

In particular, equality in (3) holds pi-almost everywhere. The u_i can
be taken Lipschitz, with ith Lipschitz constant bounded by a Lipschitz
constant L_i of c in its ith variable.

**Proof.** Couplings of fixed compactly supported marginals form a
nonempty compact set for weak convergence: a product probability
coupling times M proves nonemptiness, and compactness follows from
compactness of finite measures of fixed mass on the compact product.
The marginal conditions are closed. Thus the maximum is attained.

For completeness, the dual can be obtained without an infinite-dimensional
duality assumption. Replace K_i by the support of gamma_i. Choose a
finite maximal delta/2-separated net in K_i and use its Borel Voronoi
cells, with a fixed rule for ties. Each cell has diameter at most delta,
and every cell has positive measure: it contains the intersection of
K_i with the open delta/4-ball about its representative. Push gamma_i
onto these representatives. On these
finite sets, ordinary finite-dimensional linear programming duality
gives an optimal array coupling and numbers u_i at the representatives
satisfying (3)-(4) for the finite problem. This elementary duality is
the separating-hyperplane, or Farkas-lemma, theorem for a finite linear
program; both primal and dual optima here are finite and attained.

Replace the potentials one coordinate at a time by

    u_i(x_i)=max_(x_j, j!=i) [c(x_1,...,x_k)-sum_(j!=i)u_j(x_j)]

on their respective finite sets. Each replacement preserves feasibility
and decreases only the replaced potential. Its objective cannot fall
below the optimal primal objective, so optimality remains. After its
replacement, u_i is L_i-Lipschitz on its finite set. Later replacements
do not change this property. Normalize by adding constants of total
sum zero so that u_i at a chosen reference point is zero for i<k.
Their oscillations are uniformly bounded by L_i diam(K_i). Some tuple
of positive optimal coupling mass has equality in (3), which also
bounds the value, and hence the entire oscillation interval, of u_k.
Thus all normalized potentials are uniformly bounded.

Extend each potential from its finite set to K_i by the Lipschitz
extension

    x -> min_t [u_i(t)+L_i |x-t|].

This agrees on the finite set, is L_i-Lipschitz, and is uniformly bounded.
If x_i is in the cell represented by t_i, comparison with that tuple
shows that the sum of the extended potentials is at least
c(x_1,...,x_k)-2 delta sum_i L_i. Add 2 delta sum_i L_i to the last
potential to obtain an exactly feasible continuous dual tuple.

The finite optimal values converge to the compact optimal value as
delta tends to zero. Indeed, pushing any compact coupling to the cell
representatives changes its cost by at most M delta sum_i L_i.
Conversely, lift any finite coupling by replacing each representative
tuple with the product of the normalized restrictions of the original
marginals to its cells, times its tuple mass. This preserves every
original marginal and gives the same error bound. The continuous dual
objectives differ from the finite objectives by a quantity tending to
zero. Arzela-Ascoli now gives a subsequence of the normalized extensions
converging uniformly on every K_i. Its limit satisfies (3), and its
objective equals the compact primal maximum. Integrating the nonnegative
duality gap against an optimal coupling proves the last assertion. QED.

Only compactness and Euclidean Lipschitz extension were used here. The
sets K_i need not be convex or have interior.

## 3. A maximizing convex surplus gives Lipschitz inverse endpoint maps

Let phi:R^m->R be C^2 and uniformly strongly convex:

    D^2 phi(z) >= epsilon I       for all z, epsilon>0. (5)

Let pi maximize integral phi(b(x)) d pi among the fixed-marginal
couplings. Apply Section 2 to the smooth cost c=phi composed with b
on the compact marginal supports K_i. Obtain an attained compact
dual tuple u_i. For each i define a SEPARATE global extension, using
these original compact dual potentials:

    U_i(x)=max_(x_j in K_j, j!=i)
       [phi(lambda_i x+sum_(j!=i)lambda_j x_j)
                               -sum_(j!=i)u_j(x_j)]. (6)

For k=1 this means U_1=phi. Each U_i is finite, continuous, and
epsilon lambda_i^2-strongly convex on all R^m. Indeed every function
inside the maximum has that strong convexity constant. On K_i one has
U_i<=u_i by dual feasibility. At a tuple where equality holds in (3),
the tuple of its other coordinates realizes equality in (6), and

    U_i(x_i)=u_i(x_i),
    lambda_i grad phi(b(x)) belongs to partial U_i(x_i). (7)

For the subgradient assertion, the smooth convex function corresponding
to those fixed other coordinates lies below U_i everywhere and agrees
at x_i. Its tangent plane therefore supports U_i there. This argument
does not differentiate u_i on a possibly irregular marginal support.
We do not assert that the different global extensions together form a
globally feasible dual tuple; that assertion is unnecessary.

For clarity, a finite kappa-strongly convex function U has a conjugate
U^*(p)=sup_x[p.x-U(x)] that is finite and C^1 on all R^m, and its
gradient is 1/kappa-Lipschitz. To see this directly, U(x)-p.x is
coercive and strictly convex, so it has a unique minimizer T(p), with
p in partial U(T(p)). Strong monotonicity of its subgradients gives

    kappa |T(p)-T(q)|^2 <= (p-q).(T(p)-T(q)),

and hence the Lipschitz bound. The two maximizing-point inequalities
for U^*(p+h)-U^*(p) put it between h.T(p) and h.T(p+h). The Lipschitz
bound then proves differentiability with gradient T(p).

Apply this fact to (6), and set

    F_i(z)=grad U_i^*(lambda_i grad phi(z)).         (8)

Each F_i is locally Lipschitz. Equations (7)-(8) show that

    x_i=F_i(b(x))               for pi-almost every tuple x. (9)

Thus, for rho=b_*pi,

    (F_i)_*rho=gamma_i,
    sum_i lambda_i F_i(z)=z     for rho-almost every z. (10)

No injectivity of F_i, Monge representation of the whole coupling, or
uniqueness of an optimal coupling has been used.

## 4. The density estimate for the maximizing law

**Lemma.** Every maximizing coupling in Section 3 has a barycentric
law rho dominated by A Leb_m, with A as in (1).

**Proof.** Choose a ball containing the compact support of rho and
slightly enlarge it. The maps F_i are Lipschitz there. The area formula
for a Lipschitz map F:R^m->R^m gives, for every Borel subset E of this
ball,

    Leb_m(F(E)) <= integral_E |det DF(z)| dz.        (11)

Indeed the integral counts image points with their nonnegative integer
multiplicity, which is at least one on the image. Images of Borel sets
are analytic and universally measurable; all image-measure expressions
can equivalently be interpreted in the completed measures. By (10),

    rho(E) <= gamma_i(F_i(E))
           <= a_i Leb_m(F_i(E))
           <= a_i integral_E |det DF_i(z)| dz.      (12)

This proves absolute continuity rho=h dz and the inequalities

    h(z) <= a_i |det DF_i(z)|       almost everywhere, for every i. (13)

We justify precisely the matrices in (13). The gradient of the convex
C^1 function U_i^* is Lipschitz. Rademacher's theorem therefore gives
its derivative almost everywhere. At such points this derivative is a
symmetric positive semidefinite matrix: symmetry follows by identifying
the weak derivatives as distributional second derivatives of U_i^*,
and positivity follows from the monotonicity of its gradient. The map
z->lambda_i grad phi(z) is a C^1 diffeomorphism of R^m onto R^m with
locally Lipschitz inverse. In fact strong convexity makes grad phi
injective with globally 1/epsilon-Lipschitz inverse, and minimizing
phi(z)-p.z proves surjectivity; the inverse-function theorem applies
because D^2 phi is positive definite. Consequently the inverse image
of the exceptional null set for grad U_i^* is null. The chain rule
therefore gives, for almost every z,

    DF_i(z)=lambda_i G_i(z) H(z),
    H(z)=D^2 phi(z)>0,
    G_i(z)=D(grad U_i^*)(lambda_i grad phi(z))>=0.   (14)

Let E_0 be the closed set where sum_i lambda_i F_i(z)=z. It has full
rho measure by (10). At almost every Lebesgue density point of E_0,
all the derivatives in (14) exist and

    sum_i lambda_i DF_i(z)=I.                     (15)

Here equality is only being differentiated on E_0, which is enough:
if a differentiable function vanishes on a set having density one at
z, its derivative at z is zero. Otherwise a cone of directions where
its nonzero linear derivative is bounded away from zero would omit a
fixed positive fraction of every sufficiently small ball from that
set, a contradiction. Since rho is absolutely continuous and supported
on E_0, (14)-(15) hold rho-almost everywhere, and Lebesgue-almost
everywhere on the set where h>0.

At any such point put

    B_i=H^(1/2) DF_i H^(-1/2)
       =lambda_i H^(1/2) G_i H^(1/2).

These matrices are symmetric positive semidefinite, satisfy

    sum_i lambda_i B_i=I,
    det B_i=det DF_i>=0,                           (16)

and obey h<=a_i det B_i by (13). For a positive semidefinite m by m
matrix, the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality for its eigenvalues
gives (det B_i)^(1/m)<=tr(B_i)/m. Therefore

    h^(1/m) sum_i lambda_i a_i^(-1/m)
       <= sum_i lambda_i (det B_i)^(1/m)
       <= sum_i lambda_i tr(B_i)/m
        =1.                                       (17)

This is h<=A. At points where h=0 the assertion is automatic. QED.

In particular, no unsupported claim of Euclidean monotonicity of an
endpoint-to-endpoint map enters the determinant estimate. The common
conjugation by H^(1/2), supplied by the convex dual extensions, is the
reason all relevant matrices are positive semidefinite in the same
coordinates. The real-analysis results used here are Rademacher's
theorem, the Lipschitz area formula, Lebesgue differentiation, and the
ordinary inverse-function theorem; no transport regularity theorem is
needed.

## 5. Simultaneous convex-order domination

Let P be the compact convex set of all couplings of the given marginals,
and let

    D={pi in P: b_*pi<=A Leb_m}.                    (18)

This set is convex, compact, and nonempty. For closedness, if pi_j
converges weakly to pi, then b_*pi_j converges weakly to b_*pi, and
integrating any nonnegative compactly supported continuous function
passes the measure bound to the limit. These test inequalities imply
the same Borel measure bound. Nonemptiness follows from Section 4 by
maximizing, for example, phi(z)=|z|^2.

First fix any finite convex function f:R^m->R. Smooth it by convolution
with a nonnegative compactly supported smooth approximate identity,
and add epsilon |z|^2. The resulting functions phi_epsilon are smooth,
uniformly strongly convex (for each epsilon>0), and converge uniformly
to f on the common compact barycenter support. By Sections 3-4 an
optimal coupling pi_epsilon for phi_epsilon lies in D and satisfies

    integral phi_epsilon d rho_pi_epsilon
                 >= integral phi_epsilon d rho_pi0.

Pass to a weakly convergent subsequence in D and use uniform convergence
of the costs. This proves

    max_(pi in D) integral f d rho_pi
                 >= integral f d rho_pi0          (19)

for every individual finite convex f. The maximizer in (19) may so far
depend on f.

For finitely many convex functions f_1,...,f_r, consider the compact
convex subset of R^r

    V={(integral f_j d rho_pi-integral f_j d rho_pi0)_(j=1)^r:
                                                         pi in D}.

If V did not meet the closed positive orthant, strict separation of
that closed convex orthant from the compact convex set V would give
numbers t_j>=0, not all zero, with

    sup_(v in V) sum_j t_j v_j <0.                 (20)

To check the signs, the infimum of a separating linear functional
on the positive orthant is finite only when all its coefficients are
nonnegative; then that infimum is zero. Equation (20) contradicts
(19) for the finite convex function sum_j t_j f_j. Thus one member of
D satisfies the desired comparisons for any finite collection of
convex tests. The associated closed subsets of compact D consequently
have the finite-intersection property. Their intersection over ALL
finite convex functions is nonempty. Any member of that intersection
proves (2).

All couplings have the same barycenter first moment sum_i lambda_i
integral x d gamma_i. Hence the selected law has exactly the same
mass and first moment as the old law, not just inequalities in affine
directions. This finishes the theorem.

## 6. Anchored parallel-face application and its scope

Suppose actual convex fibers K_zi in R^d and K_p obey

    p=sum_i lambda_i z_i is a sampled integer base,
    sum_i lambda_i K_zi subset K_p,
    sum_i lambda_i h_Kzi(n)=h_Kp(n).               (21)

Take measures gamma_i of common mass M on the parallel support faces
K_zi(n), absolutely continuous with density at most a_i with respect
to m-dimensional Euclidean measure in their parallel m-dimensional
affine tangent spaces. Assume these spaces have the same tangent
subspace. Choose an orthonormal identification of that subspace with
R^m and translate the face origins compatibly. Apply the theorem to
their tangent-coordinate measures. Every tuple barycenter belongs to
the ACTUAL face K_p(n), by the inclusion and tight height in (21).
The selected law is therefore supported on the weighted affine m-plane
inside that actual face, has density at most A with respect to the
m-dimensional Euclidean measure on this plane, and dominates the old
face-barycenter law for every convex physical test. If the target face
itself has dimension m, this is domination by its face measure. If it
has larger dimension, domination by its higher-dimensional area does
not follow. No lattice label is rounded or changed.

For two actual endpoint crossflow measures each bounded by face area,
when all three faces have the same affine dimension and parallel
tangent spaces, their selected midpoint law is bounded by the area of
the actual middle face. In particular this applies to facets in every
ambient dimension. In a finite polyhedral normal
fan, selection can be carried out at each relevant normal separately;
the finite combination has no measurable-selection issue. As in the
three-fiber note, compact convex-order martingale existence then permits
rebuilding the middle transport. The coupling just constructed can be
disintegrated over its barycenter, and each tuple can be split into its
endpoints with weights lambda_i; that split has precisely its
barycenter as its conditional mean.

If instead alpha_i are target branches of masses lambda_i M with
alpha_i<=Leb_m, applying the theorem to gamma_i=alpha_i/lambda_i gives
the different constant

    A=(sum_i lambda_i^(1+1/m))^(-m).               (22)

This depends on the actual barycentric weights. It is not automatically
an integer parity factor.

The theorem assumes full-dimensional absolute continuity in the stated
tangent space. It does not identify conditional surface measures on
arbitrary nonpolyhedral normal bundles with Lebesgue measure in a face,
nor does it supply a measurable family of choices for a continuum of
normals. Such an application requires its own disintegration and
domination arguments. Intrinsically zero-dimensional face laws are
trivial point masses once their common anchored barycenter is fixed,
but the dimension-dependent formula (1) is not used with m=0.

Convex-order comparisons remain comparisons for convex functions.
They do not imply halfspace indicator comparisons. For a selected
two-endpoint coupling, the literal midpoint implication

    1_H(z_-,X_-)+1_H(z_+,X_+)
             >=1_H((z_-+z_+)/2,(X_-+X_+)/2)

still holds pointwise for every closed ambient halfspace H and hence
simultaneously for all such H after integration. Positive-mass
supporting allocations remain separate first-variation data; the
density-selection theorem does not replace them by literal indicators.

## 7. Sharpness of the density constant

Choose any compact convex body K in R^m with Leb_m(K)=1. Put

    r_i=(M/a_i)^(1/m),
    gamma_i=a_i 1_(t_i+r_i K) Leb_m.

These measures all have mass M. Couple them by taking u with measure
M 1_K du and x_i=t_i+r_i u. Its barycenter is t+R u, where

    t=sum_i lambda_i t_i,
    R=sum_i lambda_i r_i.

The resulting law has constant density M/R^m=A on t+R K. Moreover
every coupling of these same marginals has its barycenter in t+R K:
convexity gives sum_i lambda_i r_i K=R K. This set has volume R^m,
so no barycenter law of mass M supported there can have a universal
density upper bound smaller than M/R^m=A. Thus the constant is exact.

## 8. Dependency and audit ledger

The logical chain is finite compact-cost duality with attainment ->
separate strongly convex global extensions -> Lipschitz inverse
endpoint maps -> area formula and common positive-semidefinite matrix
identity -> exact density bound -> finite convex-test separation and
compactness -> one selected law dominating the prescribed old law.

The crucial support issue is handled globally in (6)-(7), rather than
by assuming interiors of the marginal supports. The derivative of the
barycentric identity is used only after absolute continuity has been
proved, at Lebesgue density points of its equality set. No Jacobian
injectivity, endpoint-map differentiability on a prescribed singular
set, or interchange of a maximum and an infinite list of tests is
assumed. The finite-intersection step is what makes all convex tests
hold for one law.

This note does not establish OC; the geometric packing, cap-allocation,
and eventual exact depth payment remain additional requirements.
